questions.prompt: Put the stages of a deployment pipeline in order.
questions.explanation: A change is committed, built, tested, packaged into an artifact, deployed, and finally released to users.

questions.prompt: Installing the right DevOps tools is enough to make a team practice DevOps, even if Dev and Ops still work in silos.
questions.explanation: DevOps is culture before tools; a siloed team with every tool gets little of the benefit.

questions.prompt: Why did the traditional wall between Dev and Ops cause friction?
choices: Dev was rewarded for shipping change while Ops was rewarded for stability
Dev and Ops used the same incentives but different tools
Ops wrote all the application code
Dev was responsible for the data center hardware
questions.answer: Dev was rewarded for shipping change while Ops was rewarded for stability
questions.explanation: Opposite incentives made each team resist the other's goals.

questions.prompt: What does continuous integration mean in practice?
choices: Merging small changes to a shared branch often, with an automated build and tests on each merge
Merging everyone's work once at the end of a release
Deploying every commit directly to users
Running tests manually before each release
questions.answer: Merging small changes to a shared branch often, with an automated build and tests on each merge
questions.explanation: CI is frequent merging backed by an automated build and test run.

questions.prompt: Merging small changes frequently tends to produce smaller, easier-to-resolve conflicts than merging large changes rarely.
questions.explanation: Branches that diverge for a long time collect more overlapping edits.

questions.prompt: What does the abbreviation CI stand for?
questions.explanation: CI is continuous integration.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes continuous deployment from continuous delivery?
choices: Deployment pushes passing changes to production automatically, while delivery keeps a manual approval before release
Delivery pushes to production automatically, while deployment requires manual approval
Deployment skips testing
Delivery only applies to databases
questions.answer: Deployment pushes passing changes to production automatically, while delivery keeps a manual approval before release
questions.explanation: Both keep changes always releasable; the difference is whether the final release is automatic or gated by a person.

questions.prompt: Match each release term to its meaning.
pairs: Two full environments with one traffic switch
Send a small slice of real traffic to the new version first
Revert to the last known-good version
Ship a new deploy that fixes the problem
questions.explanation: Blue-green and canary limit release risk; rollback and roll-forward are the two ways to respond to a bad deploy.

questions.prompt: A canary release sends 5% of traffic to the new version. Out of 2,000 requests, how many reach the canary?
An imperative script says "create a server" three times. If it is run twice on an empty environment, how many servers exist?
questions.explanation: The script just repeats its steps and does not check what exists, so two runs create 3 + 3 = 6 servers.

questions.prompt: A declarative definition states the desired end state, so applying it again to an environment that already matches it creates nothing new.
questions.explanation: The tool compares desired and actual state and only changes the difference.

questions.prompt: What is configuration drift?
choices: A running environment gradually diverging from what its definition file says
A server being moved to another region
A build failing because of a missing test
A container restarting automatically
questions.answer: A running environment gradually diverging from what its definition file says
questions.explanation: Manual changes make reality stop matching the file; IaC reconciles it back.

questions.prompt: Match each orchestration term to its meaning.
pairs: Smallest deployable unit, holding one or more containers
A set of nodes managed together
Replacing failed pods to restore the desired state
questions.explanation: Pods run on nodes, nodes form a cluster, and the orchestrator keeps reality matching the desired state.

questions.prompt: The desired state says 3 replicas, and one pod crashes. What does the orchestrator do?
choices: Starts a replacement pod to get back to 3
Does nothing until a person intervenes
Lowers the desired state to 2
Shuts down the cluster
questions.answer: Starts a replacement pod to get back to 3
questions.explanation: The orchestrator continuously compares actual to desired state and corrects differences.

questions.prompt: Explain why a team running a handful of containers by hand needs an orchestrator once the fleet grows large.
rubric: Says manual management does not scale as container count grows
Mentions scheduling or placing containers across machines
Mentions restarting failed containers or self-healing
Mentions scaling up or down with demand
questions.model: Manually starting, placing, restarting, and scaling dozens or hundreds of containers across many machines is slow and error-prone. An orchestrator automates scheduling pods onto nodes, replaces failed containers, and scales replicas to match a declared desired state.
questions.explanation: Orchestration exists to automate placement, recovery, and scaling that humans cannot do reliably at fleet scale.

questions.prompt: Match each observability signal to what it provides.
pairs: The path of a single request across services
questions.explanation: Each signal is a different window: events, numbers over time, and request journeys.

questions.prompt: An alert that pages someone at 3 a.m. with no action they can take adds fatigue without adding safety.
questions.explanation: Alerts should be actionable; otherwise people learn to ignore them.

questions.prompt: What is the incident commander's role?
choices: Coordinating the response by tracking status and deciding next steps
Writing the code fix alone
Assigning blame for the outage
Waiting for the incident to resolve itself
questions.answer: Coordinating the response by tracking status and deciding next steps
questions.explanation: The commander coordinates so that the responders do not each investigate independently.

questions.prompt: Which of these are signs a team is failing at DevOps even with the tools installed?
choices: Dev and Ops still hand work over as separate silos
Alerts nobody can act on keep paging people
Every deploy runs through the same automated pipeline
People mute alerts because of alert fatigue
A rollback plan exists and is practiced
answers: Dev and Ops still hand work over as separate silos
Alerts nobody can act on keep paging people
People mute alerts because of alert fatigue
questions.explanation: Silos and noisy, non-actionable alerts are anti-patterns; automation and rollback plans are healthy.

questions.prompt: What is the term for people ignoring or muting alerts because they fire too often?
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue is desensitization from too many or unactionable alerts.

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of a CI/CD pipeline you would design for a small web application, and say why each stage exists.
rubric: Includes a build stage and automated tests
Packages one versioned artifact reused across stages
Deploys with a safe release approach or rollback plan
questions.model: Every commit triggers an automated build and test run. A passing build is packaged as one versioned artifact, deployed to staging, then to production using a safe approach such as canary or blue-green with a rollback plan, and monitored afterward so problems are noticed quickly.
questions.explanation: A good pipeline automates build, test, packaging, safe deployment, and monitoring.
